# GLM for continuous response data {#sec-glm2}

## Gaussian GLM {#sec-glm2-gauss}

The simplest case of the GLM is the one with a Gaussian response distribution and an identity link function. In state-space notation this is:

$$y\sim Normal\left(E\left(y\right),\sigma_{res}\right)$$

$$E\left(y\right)=\eta$$

$$\eta=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{X}$$

$$\sigma_{res}>0$$

If that looks familiar, it should. A Gaussian GLM is just another way to say, "ordinary linear regression". We covered linear regression (and linear models in general) in @sec-lin-lm. Refer to @sec-lin-reg for exposition and a worked example.

## Gaussian GLM with a log link {#sec-glm2-gausslog}

If we add a log link function to the Gaussian GLM, we get a new model:

$$y\sim Normal\left(\mu,\sigma_{res}\right)$$

$$\log{\mu}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{X}$$

Just as in linear regression, the response distribution follows a normal distribution, but its expected value $\mu$ is related to the linear predictors through a log link function. This appears similar to fitting a linear regression on log-transformed $y$ variable, but it is not the same. The differences are summarized here:

| Property | `lm(log(y) ~ x)` | `glm(y ~ x, gaussian(link = "log"))` |
|---|---|---|
| Response distribution | Lognormal | Normal |
| What is modeled linearly? | $E[\log(Y)\mid x]$ | $\log(E[Y\mid x])$ |
| Error variance | Constant on log scale | Constant on original scale |
| Predicted mean on original scale | $\exp(\eta+\sigma^2/2)$ | $\exp(\eta)$ |
| Predicted median on original scale | $\exp(\eta)$ | $\exp(\eta)$ |
| Possible predicted values | Positive | Positive |
| Possible observed values under model | Positive only | Any real number |

: Comparison of a log-transformed linear model and a Gaussian GLM with a log link. In both models, $\eta=\beta_0+\beta_1x$ is the linear predictor. {#tbl-log-transform-vs-link}

That last row is very important. A log-transformed linear regression (left column) is restricted to positive observed $y$ values. The Gaussian GLM with a log link function, however, can have observed values that are negative, zero, or positive. It is only the expected value $\exp(\eta)$ that is constrained to be positive.

### Example with simulated data {#sec-glm2-gausslog-sim}

Let's explore the Gaussian GLM with log link by first simulating some data and then analyzing them.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6


set.seed(123)
n <- 50
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
beta0 <- -5.1
beta1 <- 0.8
eta <- beta0 + beta1*x
sigma <- 3
y <- rnorm(n, exp(eta), sigma)

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(x,y,pch=16)
```

At first glance, these data are a mess! A linear regression is probably inappropriate, because the pattern does not form a straight line. Worse, the variance appears to vary across the domain of $x$. We would just log-transform these data, but this would require dropping the negative values. 

Instead, we apply the Gaussian GLM with log link. This model requires you to supply some starting values for the fitting algorithm. We will supply starting means (`mustart`, for the $\mu$ term above).

```{r}
mod1 <- glm(y~x, family=gaussian(link="log"),
            mustart=rep(1,n))
```

and inspect the fitted values:

```{r}
summary(mod1)
```

Alternatively, we can try supplying guesses at the model parameters. You can supply these as a simple vector (unlike the `start` argument in `nls()`).

```{r}
mod2 <- glm(y~x, family=gaussian(link="log"),
            start=c(-3, 1))
summary(mod2)
```

If we are satisfied with that model fit, we can plot the model predictions and their 95% confidence interval (CI).

```{r}
# x values
px <- seq(min(x), max(x), length=100)
# calculate prediction
pred <- predict(mod2, newdata=data.frame(x=px),
                type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
invlink <- mod2$family$linkinv
mn <- invlink(qnorm(0.5, pred$fit, pred$se.fit))
lo <- invlink(qnorm(0.025, pred$fit, pred$se.fit))
up <- invlink(qnorm(0.975, pred$fit, pred$se.fit))


```

```{r}

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(x,y,pch=16)
points(px, lo, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(px, up, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(px, mn, type="l", lwd=2, col="red")
```

The figure above shows the behavior of the Gaussian log-link model: it constrains the predicted response to be positive, but does not constrain the observations to be positive. It seems like the 95% CI should include negative values, but remember that the CI is a statement of uncertainty about the predicted mean $\mu$, not about the whole distribution of response values. That would be a **prediction interval**.

```{r}
# 95% prediction interval
sigma_hat <- sqrt(summary(mod2)$dispersion)

# Approximate SE of fitted mean on response scale (delta method)
se_mean <- mn * pred$se.fit
lo_pred <- mn - 1.96 * sqrt(sigma_hat^2 + se_mean^2)
up_pred <- mn + 1.96 * sqrt(sigma_hat^2 + se_mean^2)

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(x,y,pch=16)
points(px, lo, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(px, up, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(px, mn, type="l", lwd=2, col="red")
points(px, up_pred, type="l", lwd=2, lty=3, col="blue")
points(px, lo_pred, type="l", lwd=2, lty=3, col="blue")
legend("topleft",
       legend=c("Confidence interval", "Prediction interval"),
       lwd=2, col=c("red", "blue"),
       lty=c(2,3), bty="n")

```


### Example with real data {#sec-glm2-gausslog-real}

Let's use the NEON data for a quick example. Download the [site-level richness and environmental dataset](../datasets/dat-neon-site-rich-env.csv) and put it in your working directory.

```{r}
#| include: false
dx <- read.csv("../datasets/dat-neon-site-rich-env.csv")
```


```{r}
#| eval: false
dx <- read.csv("dat-neon-site-rich-env.csv")
```

We expect that mean annual temperature (`dx$mat`) should decrease with latitude, and a scatterplot confirms that:

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(dx$lat, dx$mat,
     xlab=expression(Latitude~(degree*N)),
     ylab=expression(Mean~annual~temp~(degree*C)),
     pch=16)
```

This seems pretty linear, but there might be some heteroscedasticity issues in the middle latitudes. Let's fit an ordinary linear regression and a Guassian log-link GLM.

```{r}
mod1 <- lm(mat~lat, data=dx)
mod2 <- glm(mat~lat, data=dx, family=gaussian(link="log"),
            start=c(5, -0.05))
```

```{r}
summary(mod1)
```

```{r}
summary(mod2)
```

Compare the two model predictions:

```{r}
px <- seq(min(dx$lat), max(dx$lat))
prx <- data.frame(lat=px)
pred1 <- predict(mod1, newdata=prx, se.fit=TRUE)
pred2 <- predict(mod2, newdata=prx, type="link", se.fit=TRUE)

prx$lo1 <- qnorm(0.025, pred1$fit, pred1$se.fit)
prx$mn1 <- qnorm(0.5, pred1$fit, pred1$se.fit)
prx$up1 <- qnorm(0.975, pred1$fit, pred1$se.fit)

prx$lo2 <- exp(qnorm(0.025, pred2$fit, pred2$se.fit))
prx$mn2 <- exp(qnorm(0.5, pred2$fit, pred2$se.fit))
prx$up2 <- exp(qnorm(0.975, pred2$fit, pred2$se.fit))
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(dx$lat, dx$mat,
     xlab=expression(Latitude~(degree*N)),
     ylab=expression(Mean~annual~temp~(degree*C)),
     pch=16)
points(prx$lat, prx$lo1, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(prx$lat, prx$up1, type="l", lwd=2, lty=2, col="red")
points(prx$lat, prx$mn1, type="l", lwd=2,        col="red")
points(prx$lat, prx$lo2, type="l", lwd=2, lty=3, col="blue")
points(prx$lat, prx$up2, type="l", lwd=2, lty=3, col="blue")
points(prx$lat, prx$mn2, type="l", lwd=2,        col="blue")
legend("topright",
       legend=c("LM",
                "Gaussian log-link GLM"),
       lwd=2, col=c("red", "blue"),
       lty=c(2,3), bty="n")
```

## Gamma GLM {#sec-glm2-gamma}

This section explores GLMs for data following a **gamma distribution**.
Gamma-distributed data can show up in two ways in biology: waiting
times, or overdispersed continuous data (i.e., data where
$\sigma > \mu$). The latter case may also be well-modeled by a [Gaussian GLM with log-link](@sec-glm2-gausslog), but the gamma GLM offers an elegant (and under-utilized) alternative.

**Gamma regression** is a GLM where response values follow a gamma
distribution. The gamma distribution usually describes one of two kinds
of data: waiting times until a certain number of events occur, or
right-skewed continuous data. The gamma distribution is the continuous
analogue of the negative binomial distribution. The figure below shows
this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4


# gamma vs. negative binomial figure
# shape = k = number of events
# scale = theta = time until events
x1 <- seq(0, 20, length=100)
y1 <- dgamma(x1, shape=2, scale=2)

# mu = mean
# size = 2
x2 <- 0:20
y2 <- dnbinom(x2, size=4, prob=0.5)

par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1), 
    bty="n", lend=1, las=1, cex.axis=1.3, 
    cex.lab=1.3)
plot(x1, y1, type="l", lwd=3,
     xlab="Value", ylab="Probability density")
text(10, 0.12, expression("Gamma"*(list(italic(a)==2,italic(s)==2))), 
     adj=0, cex=1, xpd=NA)
text(10, 0.1, expression(italic(a)==Shape),adj=0, cex=1)
text(10, 0.085, expression(italic(s)==Scale),adj=0, cex=1)
plot(x2, y2, pch=16, cex=1.2,
     xlab="Value", ylab="Probability mass")
text(8, 0.1, expression(NB*(list(italic(n)==4, italic(p)==0.5))),adj=0, cex=1)
text(8, 0.085, expression(italic(n)==Size),adj=0, cex=1)
text(8, 0.07, expression(italic(p)==Prob),adj=0, cex=1)
```

A gamma distribution with shape *a* and scale *s* is basically a
continuous version of a negative binomial distribution with size *n* and
probability *p* according to the following relationships:

$$a=\frac{\mu^2}{\sigma^2}$$

$$s=\frac{\mu}{a}$$

Where $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ can be calculated from the parameters of the
negative binomial distribution as:

$$\mu=\frac{n\left(1-p\right)}{p}$$

$$\sigma^2=\frac{n\left(1-p\right)}{p^2}$$

The relationships above can be used to convert between gamma distributions and negative binomial distributions with other parameterizations. For example, ecologists often use an alternate version of the negative binomial with mean $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}=\mu + (\mu^{2}/k)$.

Like the negative binomial, biologists can take advantage of the numerical properties of the gamma to model phenomena for which the variance is much greater than the mean. The gamma distribution can only take on nonnegative values, so if you have negative values you may not be able to use it.

### Example with simulated data {#sec-glm2-gamma-sim}

As always, we will start with analysis of simulated data. Notice that we
are using **log link function**. The canonical link for the gamma
distribution is the **reciprocal function** ($f(x)=1/x$). However, the
reciprocal function is more applicable for the "waiting time"
interpretation of the distribution. For the "right-skewed non-negative
distribution" interpretation, the log or identity links can be
appropriate. However, the log-link cannot be used if your data contain
0s.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 30
x <- round(runif(n, 0, 4), 1)

# coefficients
beta0 <- 0.9
beta1 <- 1.2

# linear predictor
eta <- beta0 + beta1 * x

# inverse link
y <- exp(eta)

# gamma parameter
shape <- 4

# draw y values (stochastic part)
y <- rgamma(n, rate=shape/y, shape=shape)

# assemble dataset
dat <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)
```

Now, take a look at the data.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6
plot(x,y)
```

The relationship looks like it might be log-linear---i.e., linear on a
logarithmic scale. We can check that with another scatterplot:

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6
plot(x, log(y))
```

When *y* is log-transformed, things look linear. We will try a Gaussian
GLM with log link function. Because the variance looks like it increases
at larger *X* values, we will also try a gamma GLM. One characteristic
of the gamma distribution is that the variance is proportional to the
mean squared, which might be the case here.

```{r}
mod1 <- glm(y~x, data=dat, family=gaussian(link="log"))
summary(mod1)
```

```{r}
mod2 <- glm(y~x, data=dat, family=Gamma(link="log"))
summary(mod2)
```

Notice that the parameter estimates from the gamma GLM were much closer
to "reality" than those of the Gaussian GLM. Which model performed
better? The pseudo-*R*^2^ suggests the gamma:

```{r}
1-mod1$deviance/mod1$null.deviance
```

```{r}
1-mod2$deviance/mod2$null.deviance
```

The best test is to plot the predicted values against the actual values
and compare the models.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

# values for prediction
use.n <- 50
px <- seq(min(x), max(x), length=use.n)

# calculate predictions and CI
pred1 <- predict(mod1, newdata=data.frame(x=px),
                 type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
mn1 <- pred1$fit
lo1 <- qnorm(0.025, mn1, pred1$se.fit)
up1 <- qnorm(0.975, mn1, pred1$se.fit)

# inverse link function
mn1 <- mod1$family$linkinv(mn1)
lo1 <- mod1$family$linkinv(lo1)
up1 <- mod1$family$linkinv(up1)

# calculate predictions and CI for gamma model
pred2 <- predict(mod2, newdata=data.frame(x=px),
                 type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
mn2 <- pred1$fit
lo2 <- qnorm(0.025, mn2, pred2$se.fit)
up2 <- qnorm(0.975, mn2, pred2$se.fit)

# inverse link function
mn2 <- mod1$family$linkinv(mn2)
lo2 <- mod1$family$linkinv(lo2)
up2 <- mod1$family$linkinv(up2)

# make plot
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(x,y, main="Normal GLM")
polygon(x=c(px, rev(px)), y=c(lo1, rev(up1)),
        border=NA, col="grey80")
points(px, mn1, type="l", lwd=3)
points(x, y)
plot(x,y, main="Gamma GLM")
polygon(x=c(px, rev(px)), y=c(lo2, rev(up2)),
        border=NA, col="grey80")
points(px, mn2, type="l", lwd=3)
points(x, y)
```

The gamma GLM captured the heteroscedasticity in the data (non-constant
variance) better than the Gaussian (normal) GLM. We should conclude that
the gamma GLM better represents the data. If you have a heteroscedastic
relationship that isn't well-modeled by other GLMs, the gamma GLM might
be worth a try.

### Example with real data {#sec-glm2-gamma-real}

Returning to the NEON data, consider this plot of net primary productivity vs. latitude. If you don't already have it, download the [site-level richness and environmental dataset](../datasets/dat-neon-site-rich-env.csv) and put it in your working directory.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(dx$lat, dx$npp,
     xlab=expression(Latitude~(degree*N)),
     ylab=expression(g~C~m^{-2}~yr^{-1}))
```

There is clearly a negative trend, but a linear model might be inappropriate because of how much variance there is around the middle latitudes. This is a sampling bias: most NEON sites are in the continental US, which is largely between 30 and 50 degrees north latitude. Still, the heteroscedasticity is there and need to account for it. Let's try a gamma GLM.

```{r}
mod3 <- glm(npp~lat, data=dx, family=Gamma(link="log"))
summary(mod3)
```

The pseudo-$R^2$ is encouraging:

```{r}
1-mod3$deviance/mod3$null.deviance
```

Let's check the model predictions:

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

# values for prediction
use.n <- 50
px <- seq(min(dx$lat), max(dx$lat), length=use.n)

# calculate predictions and CI
pred <- predict(mod3, newdata=data.frame(lat=px),
                 type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
mn <- qnorm(0.5, pred$fit, pred$se.fit)
lo <- qnorm(0.025, pred$fit, pred$se.fit)
up <- qnorm(0.975, pred$fit, pred$se.fit)

# inverse link function
mn <- mod3$family$linkinv(mn)
lo <- mod3$family$linkinv(lo)
up <- mod3$family$linkinv(up)

# make plot
par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(dx$lat, dx$npp,
     xlab=expression(Latitude~(degree*N)),
     ylab=expression(NPP~(g~C~m^{-2}~yr^{-1})),
     ylim=c(0, 3000))
polygon(x=c(px, rev(px)),
        y=c(lo, rev(up)),
        border=NA, col="grey80")
points(px, mn, type="l", lwd=3)
points(dx$lat, dx$npp, pch=16)
```

Compare the gamma GLM fit to a Gaussian log-link GLM:

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6
#| echo: false

mod4 <- glm(npp~lat, data=dx, family=gaussian(link="log"))
# calculate predictions and CI
pred4 <- predict(mod4, newdata=data.frame(lat=px),
                 type="link", se.fit=TRUE)
mn4 <- qnorm(0.5, pred4$fit, pred4$se.fit)
lo4 <- qnorm(0.025, pred4$fit, pred4$se.fit)
up4 <- qnorm(0.975, pred4$fit, pred4$se.fit)

# inverse link function
mn4 <- mod4$family$linkinv(mn4)
lo4 <- mod4$family$linkinv(lo4)
up4 <- mod4$family$linkinv(up4)

# make plot
par(mar=c(5.1, 5.1, 1.1, 1.1))
plot(dx$lat, dx$npp,
     xlab=expression(Latitude~(degree*N)),
     ylab=expression(NPP~(g~C~m^{-2}~yr^{-1})),
     ylim=c(0, 3000))
points(px, lo4, type="l", lwd=2, col="red", lty=2)
points(px, up4, type="l", lwd=2, col="red", lty=2)
points(px, mn4, type="l", lwd=2, col="red")
points(px, lo4, type="l", lwd=2, col="blue", lty=3)
points(px, up4, type="l", lwd=2, col="blue", lty=3)
points(px, mn4, type="l", lwd=2, col="blue")
points(dx$lat, dx$npp, pch=16)
legend("topright",
       legend=c("Gamma GLM",
                "Gaussian log-link GLM"),
       lwd=2, col=c("red", "blue"),
       lty=c(2,3), bty="n")

```
